papers.title: Tau-driven hyperexcitability of locus coeruleus noradrenergic neurons underlies sleep fragmentation and cognitive decline in mice.
papers.abstract: Early sleep disruption is a hallmark of preclinical Alzheimer's disease (AD), but its underlying mechanisms are unclear. The locus coeruleus (LC) dopamine-β-hydroxylase noradrenergic (LCDBH) neurons are vulnerable to early tau pathology in AD. Using P301S transgenic mice and cell-type-specific tau overexpression models, we show that pathological tau accumulation selectively increases the intrinsic excitability of LCDBH neurons. Tau-induced neuronal hyperactivity disrupts sleep homeostasis, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and slow-wave activity, increases sleep fragmentation and microarousals, and delays both anesthetic induction and sleep onset. Furthermore, tau overexpression in LCDBH neurons leads to significant recognition memory deficits. Notably, optogenetic suppression of LCDBH-tau neuronal activity reverses sleep disturbances and rescues cognitive dysfunction. Our findings demonstrate that tau-driven hyperexcitability of LCDBH neurons is a core driver of early sleep and cognitive impairments in AD, providing a mechanistic insight and potential target for preclinical AD treatment.

papers.title: Thalamic stereo-EEG detects sleep stages N2 and N3 with discrimination approaching scalp EEG
papers.abstract: Sleep and epilepsy interact strongly during sleep stages N2 and N3, when synchronization of brain rhythms is increased. Sleep staging relies on scalp EEG, which is often absent or incomplete during stereo-EEG monitoring and unavailable from implanted devices, while thalamic leads are increasingly implanted for epilepsy neuromodulation. Given the role of the thalamus in spindle generation and slow oscillation dynamics, we hypothesized that thalamic channels would identify N2 and N3 (N2+N3) better than other intracranial sites. We analyzed 477 h of stereo-EEG with simultaneous scalp EEG from six adults, including 46 thalamic bipolar channels on 11 electrodes. Two classifiers were evaluated on identical channels: a random forest with hidden Markov decoding (RF + HMM) trained leave-one-participant-out, and the pretrained SleepSEEG algorithm developed without thalamic channels. The primary endpoint was discrimination of N2+N3 from other stages as classified from scalp EEG by a sleep expert. Among regions sampled in all participants, thalamic channels performed best (area under the curve [AUC] 0.94 with RF + HMM and 0.93 with SleepSEEG across whole recordings; 0.88 and 0.86 at night). With RF + HMM, thalamic channels outperformed mesial temporal and temporal neocortical channels in all six participants across whole recordings. The advantage persisted against channel-count-matched subsets and a white-matter control with both classifiers. Individual thalamic electrodes reached AUCs of 0.79-0.99 with RF + HMM (10 of 11 at least 0.89). These offline findings support thalamic N2+N3 detection and motivate real-time evaluation for sleep-targeted neuromodulation.

papers.title: Adapting Sleep Foundation Models for Dense Sleep Spindle Localization
papers.abstract: Adapting sleep foundation models to dense electroencephalography (EEG) event localization is challenging because multi-second representations may not preserve sufficient temporal detail for precise boundary recovery. We address sleep spindle localization by adapting a frozen SleepFM encoder with a local time-frequency pathway that preserves spindle-relevant spectral content and intra-token position. The local representation drives localization, while residual cross-attention incorporates SleepFM temporal context. Dense predictions are obtained through localized token-to-sample reconstruction and temporal refinement. Tested on the Massive Online Data Annotation (MODA), the proposed model achieves an event-level $F_1$ of $0.8080 \pm 0.0040$ at IoU 0.2 across six folds. Ablations show that localization primarily depends on local spectral and sub-token temporal information, while the pretrained representation provides complementary context. These results indicate that dense adaptation benefits from preserving information below the pretrained token scale. Code will be released upon acceptance.

papers.title: Glial Control of Insomnia: Astrocyte-Microglia Interactions in Stress, Hyperarousal and Sleep Dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is a highly prevalent and burdensome sleep disorder whose pathophysiology remains incompletely understood. While traditional models have emphasized neuronal hyperarousal, accumulating evidence indicates that glial cells-particularly astrocytes and microglia-play central and complementary roles in the regulation of sleep-wake dynamics and the persistence of chronic insomnia. This review synthesizes clinical, experimental and translational evidence supporting a dual regulatory framework in which astrocytes and microglia act as key integrators of stress signalling, neuroinflammation, synaptic plasticity and sleep homeostasis. Astrocytes emerge as primary modulators of metabolic and neuro-modulatory coupling within sleep-wake circuits, linking hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation to dysregulated adenosine signalling, excitatory-inhibitory imbalance, impaired glymphatic clearance and circadian misalignment. In parallel, microglia function as immune and synaptic sculptors, with chronic sleep disturbance biasing them toward maladaptive activation states characterized by altered cytokine release, disrupted synaptic pruning and stress hormone-dependent signalling cascades. Although direct glia-resolved evidence in human insomnia remains limited, convergent findings from neuroimaging, animal models and sleep-immune research support a coordinated stress-glia-insomnia axis. We further highlight mechanisms of astrocyte-microglia crosstalk, including purinergic signalling, inflammatory feedback loops and calcium-dependent network synchronization, which may stabilize pathological hyperarousal states. Finally, we discuss emerging glia-targeted therapeutic strategies and key translational challenges, emphasizing the need for cell-type-specific biomarkers, spatiotemporally precise interventions and personalized treatment frameworks.

papers.title: Anti-correlation time-frequency synergy and dual-granularity fusion for sleep stage classification.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep stage classification is crucial for diagnosing sleep disorders and evaluating sleep quality. Single-channel EEG sleep staging using central electrodes has garnered significant interest due to its ability to detect a higher number of sleep spindles and its cost-effectiveness. Nevertheless, several challenges remain, such as the neglect of interdependencies among features, reduced model sensitivity to the dispersion across features, potential information leakage during the learning of transition rules, and class imbalance. To address these challenges, this study specifically designs an automatic sleep staging network based on single-channel EEG. The network incorporates a multi-branch feature extraction module, which captures negatively correlated frequency features that exhibit significant variations during sleep transitions and promotes synergistic complementarity. Furthermore, a dual-granularity residual attention mechanism is employed to perform adaptive fusion along both temporal and channel dimensions based on statistical measures such as the mean and standard deviation. The causal transition-aware network ensures temporal consistency while facilitating effective learning of transition rules. The focal loss function is utilized to counteract class imbalance. Experiments on SleepEDF-20, SleepEDF-78 and SHHS datasets show that our method achieves the best performance with overall accuracy of 87.0%, 83.4% and 84.5%, respectively. For N1 stage classification which is more challenging, it reaches an accuracy of 57.5%, 52.5% and 49.3% on three datasets, respectively. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and its certain advantages over existing methods.

papers.title: Effects of environmental enrichment and social isolation in preclinical rodent models: role of the endocannabinoid system.
papers.abstract: Environmental enrichment (EE) and social isolation (SI) represent contrasting forms of environmental manipulation that differentially engage homeostatic mechanisms and exert profound effects on brain function, behaviour, and health. Both EE and SI have been shown to modulate the endocannabinoid (EC) system, a key lipid signalling system involved in maintaining homeostasis and regulating diverse physiological and pathological processes. This review provides an overview of preclinical animal studies investigating the role of the EC system in the effects of EE and SI. The available evidence indicates that both EE and SI significantly alter EC signalling, with EE most commonly associated with increased CB1 receptor expression, whereas SI is associated with disrupted CB1 receptor functionality and dysregulated EC signalling. These effects are region-specific, influenced by the type and duration of environmental manipulation, developmental stage, underlying pathology and possibly sex. Pharmacological and genetic manipulation studies further implicate CB1 receptor signalling in mediating some of the beneficial effects of EE and reduced CB1 signalling in the detrimental consequences of SI on behaviour. Overall, the findings support a role for the EC system as an important mediator through which EE and SI modulate neural plasticity and behavioural outcomes. Further mechanistic and translational studies, including both sexes and relevant disease models, are needed to determine how these mechanisms may inform future prevention and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Physiological Sleep Features Associated With Dimensions of Daily Dysfunction in Insomnia.
papers.abstract: Daily dysfunction is a key criterion of insomnia, but its underlying structure and relationship with objective sleep physiology remain unclear. This study aimed to identify the dimensions of subjective daily dysfunction using exploratory factor analysis (EFA) in individuals with insomnia and to examine its association with polysomnography (PSG) macroarchitecture, electroencephalographic (EEG) spectral power and odds ratio product (ORP)-based sleep depth in individuals with and without insomnia. We hypothesized that more severe daily dysfunction would be associated with poorer sleep continuity, higher high-frequency EEG activity and lighter sleep depth. The final sample included 859 adults (50.1% female; mean age 44.2 ± 14.1 years) in the Sleep Apnea Global Interdisciplinary Consortium (SAGIC) without obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) or shift work, including 368 with insomnia. EFA supported a single factor underlying the nine daily dysfunction items, which were combined into a total score. In univariate linear regression analyses adjusted for age, sex and site, higher beta-1 power and several ORP measures were nominally associated with more severe daily dysfunction, but none of them survived correction for multiple comparisons. No significant predictor-by-group interactions were observed. Across three levels of sleep physiology-PSG macroarchitecture, spectral power, and continuous sleep depth-no sleep measure was associated with daily dysfunction after correction for multiple comparisons. PSG macroarchitecture and sleep EEG-derived measures may not fully capture daily dysfunction. Future studies could examine whether within-night sleep dynamics are more informative than whole-night averages.

papers.title: Slow power-envelope associations among brain, heart, and gut signals during sleep: an exploratory multivariate transfer entropy study.
papers.abstract: Sleep and the brain-gut axis both involve the coordinated regulation of the central nervous system (CNS), autonomic nervous system (ANS), and enteric nervous system. Although the role of the brain-gut axis in sleep regulation is increasingly recognized, the dynamic information flow and its directionality among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep remain unclear as statistical associations. In this study, based on overnight sleep data from 24 healthy subjects, we simultaneously collected occipital electroencephalogram (EEG), electrocardiogram, and bowel sound signals, constructed a multimodal physiological signal analysis framework, and employed a multivariate transfer entropy method based on non-uniform embedding and k-nearest neighbor estimation to systematically quantify directed statistical associations at the level of slow power envelope co-modulations among the brain, heart, and gut systems within the framework of sleep staging. The results reveal a consistent pattern of directed statistical associations: information transfer from heart to brain, brain to gut, and heart to gut consistently exceeds that in the reverse directions across all sleep stages. Sleep-stage dynamics further dissociate within-system from inter-system information flow: internal information exchange within the brain and gut intensifies with sleep depth and weakens during REM, whereas inter-system pathways show divergent stage-dependent patterns: heart-to-brain flow increases from light to deep sleep, while heart-to-gut and brain-to-gut flow are suppressed during deep sleep. At the frequency-band level, the brain, heart, and gut each exhibit dynamically reorganized source-receiver roles across sleep stages, with specific frequency bands contributing differentially to each inter-system pathway depending on sleep stage. This study identifies exploratory statistical patterns of directional information flow among the brain, heart, and gut systems during sleep, providing hypothesis-generating observations for future studies on sleep and multi-organ interactions. These directed associations do not establish anatomical pathways, causal regulation, or clinical biomarkers, and should be regarded as exploratory.

papers.title: Temporal Associations Between Physiological Sleep and Next-Day Pain Intensity in Individuals With Activity-Limiting Chronic Pain: A Multiple Night At-Home Ear-EEG Sleep-Monitoring Study.
papers.abstract: Chronic pain and sleep disturbances frequently co-occur. However, most prior research relies on self-report or actigraphy, which reflect behavioural aspects of sleep but provide only limited insight into the underlying sleep physiology. In this pre-registered prospective observational study (NCT06368531), we investigated within-person night-to-night variability in physiological sleep metrics and explored temporal associations between sleep metrics and next-day pain. Individuals with bothersome (n = 4) or high-impact (n = 15) chronic pain completed between 11 and 33 nights of at-home sleep monitoring using an ear-EEG device and rated morning pain intensity daily on a 0-10 numerical rating scale. This design enables assessment of real-world physiological sleep patterns alongside natural fluctuations in pain, offering a high-resolution view of sleep-pain dynamics beyond traditional diary or actigraphy-based methods. Substantial between-night variability was observed across multiple sleep metrics, such as sleep efficiency and sleep stage transitions (ICC values < 0.5), indicating that less than half of the total variance was attributable to differences between subjects, underscoring the importance of longitudinal within-person monitoring. Mixed-effects model analyses revealed that lower next-day pain intensity was associated with greater duration (β = -0.01, p = 0.005), higher percentage (β = -0.07, p = 0.001) and increased stability (β = -0.01, p = 0.013) of N3 sleep. In contrast, higher next-day pain was associated with increased N3 fragmentation (β = 0.01, p = 0.014) and a higher proportion of N1 sleep (β = 0.014, p = 0.007). Together, these findings provide objective physiological support for previously reported associations between sleep and pain, highlighting the value of longitudinal ear-EEG monitoring for capturing nightly sleep-pain dynamics. Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06368531.

papers.title: The Role of Drosophila Toll Receptors in the Central Nervous System.
papers.abstract: Toll-like receptors (TLRs) are evolutionarily conserved pattern recognition receptors that play pivotal roles in innate immunity by detecting pathogen-associated molecular patterns. While initially characterized for their function in dorsoventral patterning and antifungal defense in Drosophila, the Toll family is now understood to have undergone a functional expansion in the nervous system. This review synthesizes the current understanding of the nine Drosophila Toll receptors (Toll-1 to Toll-9) and their roles in the central nervous system (CNS). We discuss how these receptors, particularly through non-canonical signaling pathways, function as neurotrophin receptors and cell surface recognition molecules. They mediate a wide range of cellular processes, from axon guidance to synaptic partner matching and the regulation of neuronal survival versus apoptosis through the competitive recruitment of adaptor proteins such as dMyD88 and Sarm. We further explore the involvement of Toll signaling in adult brain structural plasticity, sleep homeostasis, and behavioral responses to environmental stressors such as ethanol. Importantly, this article addresses the context-dependent duality of Toll signaling in neuropathology, dysregulation, and aberrant activation, which are closely related to neurodegeneration, lifespan determination, and infection responses. Through this timely summary of current research, this review highlights the molecular switches that govern Toll receptor functional states and their roles in neuro-immune interactions, with implications for understanding neurological diseases in vertebrates.

papers.title: Dynamics of Sleep Architecture and Nocturnal Oxygen Saturation During Acclimatization at Intermediate Altitude: A Longitudinal Observational Study in Elite Athletes.
papers.abstract: Athletes typically undergo training camps living and sleeping at intermediate altitudes (1500-2500 m). Hypoxia reshapes sleep through central circuits regulating arousal, chemoreflex gain and sympathetic outflow. However, the relationship between peripheral oxygen saturation (SpO2) and sleep architecture and how it co-evolves during acclimatization, is unclear. We tested whether SpO2 differs across sleep stages at intermediate altitude and whether its recovery is stage specific. Seventeen mogul-ski athletes (seven women) travelled from Montréal (Canada) to Tignes (France) for a 2-week altitude training camp (AltitudeCamp; 2100 m) in June 2025. During the first week (6 nights) and the last night of AltitudeCamp, athletes were provided with a validated ring pulse oximeter and an electroencephalography (EEG) headband. We evaluated the changes in sleep stage distribution across successive nights, scored on 30-second epochs and synchronized with oximetry data. Model estimates are reported as mean ± Standard Error (SE), raw data as mean ± Standard Deviation (SD). Average total sleep time was 429 ± 47 min (mean ± SD) and did not change during AltitudeCamp (p = 0.939). Across the first week, %N3 decreased logarithmically (β = -2.35 ± 0.72%/ln (night), p = 0.002) and %Rapid eye movement sleep (REM) increased logarithmically (β = 3.13 ± 0.88%/ln (night), p < 0.001), with no changes in %Wake, %N1, or %N2. SpO2 was lower during AltitudeCamp (95.2 ± 0.3%) than measures obtained in normoxia (98 ± 0.4%; p < 0.001), and overnight heart rate (HR) was 7 ± 2 beats per minute (bpm) higher than the habitual 58 ± 3 bpm observed in normoxia (p = 0.005). Wake SpO2 increased by 0.13 ± 0.01 percentage points per night (p < 0.001), with faster recovery in N1 (0.19 ± 0.02 percentage points/night; p = 0.006) and REM (0.23 ± 0.01 percentage points/night; p < 0.001), while N2 and N3 did not differ from Wake. HR declined by 0.79 bpm/night during Wake, similar to N3 (p = 0.26), but larger than the decline in N1 (p = 0.024) and REM (p < 0.001). In N2, HR did not evolve during the first week at altitude. At intermediate altitude, nocturnal SpO2 and HR show sleep-stage-specific dynamics that mirror central ventilatory and autonomic adaptation to hypoxia. Our data suggest that acclimatization is not uniform across sleep stages, and that the first 2 nights after ascent may capture the most rapid adjustments despite similar total sleep duration. Sleep therefore offers a heterogeneous and ecologically valid index of central nervous system (CNS) acclimatization, which can be monitored longitudinally with wearable EEG-oximetry.

papers.title: Poststroke sleep phenotypes and executive dysfunction: toward a sleep-network-executive framework.
papers.abstract: Post-stroke sleep disturbance and executive dysfunction frequently coexist, yet the mechanisms linking disturbed sleep to cognitive recovery remain poorly understood. A major challenge is phenotypic heterogeneity: insomnia, sleep fragmentation, obstructive sleep apnea, hypersomnolence, and circadian disruption differ in their biological drivers and cognitive consequences. To develop a testable network-level account, we conducted a targeted synthesis of clinical stroke studies, stroke neuroimaging research, non-stroke sleep-network evidence, and intervention studies, mapping each evidence stream according to its proximity to the proposed pathway. The synthesis indicates that focal lesions, diaschisis, and structural disconnection after stroke can disrupt the integrity and coordination of the salience, default mode, and frontoparietal networks. Clinical studies support an association between disturbed sleep and poorer post-stroke cognition, while neuroimaging findings demonstrate altered large scale network organization in post-stroke cognitive impairment. Evidence from non-stroke populations further suggests that sleep loss, insomnia, and sleep fragmentation can impair network segregation, default mode regulation, frontoparietal recruitment, and salience-network-mediated switching. We therefore propose that sleep fragmentation, insomnia, and arousal instability may act as functional stressors on an already vulnerable post-stroke network architecture. Inefficient switching may permit context-inappropriate persistence of default mode activity and reduce or delay frontoparietal engagement during executive demand, thereby contributing to impaired conflict monitoring, working memory, processing speed, and cognitive flexibility. No study has directly tested this complete pathway within a single stroke cohort. The framework should therefore be regarded as a falsifiable mechanistic hypothesis rather than an established causal model. Future studies should combine objective sleep phenotyping, dynamic and effective connectivity, task based neuroimaging, domain specific executive measures, and longitudinal or interventional designs within the same stroke cohorts.

papers.title: Poor Test-Retest Stability of Nocturnal REM Sleep Onset Markers in Narcolepsy Type 1.
papers.abstract: To assess the test-retest stability of nocturnal sleep-onset REM periods (nSOREMPs) in untreated patients with narcolepsy type 1 (NT1), and of nocturnal direct REM (nDREM) transitions and their clinical and biological correlates. We included consecutive children and adults with NT1 diagnosed according to ICSD-3-TR criteria based on excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, multiple sleep latency test (MSLT) findings, or CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency, without using nSOREMPs for diagnosis. All patients underwent two untreated overnight polysomnographic (PSG). nSOREMP was defined as REM sleep within 15 minutes of sleep onset, and nDREM as direct transition from wakefulness or N1 to REM sleep without intervening N2 or N3 sleep. Among 227 patients (108 males; mean age 31.6 years (SD=14.8)), nSOREMPs were present on both PSGs in 41.8%, on one only in 35.7%, and absent on both in 22.4%, yielding poor test-retest agreement (κ=0.26, 95% CI 0.14-0.39, McNemar test p=0.10). Persistent nSOREMPs were associated with younger age, shorter sleep latency, more SOREMPs on the MSLT, and lower hypocretin levels, but not with PSG interval, symptom severity, or medication history. nDREM was present on both PSGs in 15.9%, on one PSG in 37.4%, and absent on both in 46.7%, with poor stability and persistence associated with younger age, shorter MSLT sleep latency, and lower CSF hypocretin levels. nSOREMPs and nDREMs showed limited test-retest stability in untreated children and adults with NT1. Their association with age, MSLT findings, and hypocretin levels suggest variable REM dysregulation rather than stable individual traits. Absence of nSOREMP even on two PSG should not exclude NT1.

papers.title: Affective burden and resting-state EEG microstate dynamics in sleep-severity-matched chronic insomnia.
papers.abstract: Clinical heterogeneity in chronic insomnia disorder may partly reflect affective symptom burden, but its neurophysiological correlates are difficult to distinguish from those of insomnia severity. We examined whether resting-state electroencephalographic microstate dynamics differed between affective-burden phenotypes with comparable subjective sleep severity. Among 125 treatment-naive adults with chronic insomnia disorder, 21 pairs (n = 42) with low versus high affective burden, defined using prespecified Hamilton Anxiety and Depression Rating Scale thresholds, were matched 1:1 on standardized Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and Insomnia Severity Index scores. Resting-state electroencephalographic microstate features were compared between groups using linear models adjusted for residual subjective sleep severity. Further exploratory analyses of eyes-open features examined symptom associations and full-cohort dimensional associations, and evaluated classification using leave-one-pair-out cross-validation. During eyes-open rest, the high-affective-burden phenotype showed greater microstate C coverage and lower microstate D coverage, occurrence, and duration. Microstate C coverage correlated positively with a composite affective score, whereas microstate D occurrence correlated negatively with anxiety, depression, and composite affective scores. Eyes-closed analyses showed a similar trend, but the differences did not reach statistical significance. A four-feature linear support vector classifier yielded a cross-validated area under the curve of 74.8%. Corresponding effects were directionally concordant but attenuated to non-significance in full-cohort dimensional models. Although limited by the small matched sample and reliance on questionnaire-based sleep severity without objective sleep monitoring, these findings suggest that C/D microstate dynamics may be associated with affective heterogeneity in chronic insomnia. This potential association warrants further investigation in larger cohorts incorporating objective sleep measures, while the exploratory classification findings require independent external validation.

papers.title: CLEC1B and RAC1 in peripheral immune remodeling associated with sleep disturbance: an exploratory integrative study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbance is closely linked to immune dysfunction, but the molecular features of associated peripheral immune remodeling remain incompletely defined. In this exploratory study, we integrated blood eQTL data and GWAS summary statistics with mouse PBMC single-cell data, a human PBMC transcriptome cohort, and mouse PBMC measurements. The single-cell dataset comprised one control, one 24-hour sleep-deprivation, and one 48-hour sleep-deprivation library. Descriptive single-cell patterns showed contraction of the B-cell compartment and expansion of granulocytes. Mendelian randomization nominally prioritized RAC1 and CLEC1B, with limited co-localization support. Both genes showed lower expression in the human cohort and were associated with altered B-cell communication and metabolic states. In mouse PBMCs (n = 3 per group), Clec1b qPCR showed a downward trend (P = 0.072), whereas Rac1 qPCR expression was lower after sleep deprivation (P = 0.017). Lane-level western blot analysis also showed lower CLEC1B (P = 0.0056) and RAC1 (P = 0.0016) protein abundance. These exploratory integrative analyses nominate CLEC1B and RAC1 as candidate genes associated with peripheral B-cell remodeling in a sleep-disturbance context. These hypothesis-generating findings warrant targeted functional studies of their roles in sleep-related immune remodeling.

papers.title: Tryptophan metabolism circadian regulation: clinical and pharmacological implications.
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous systems that synchronize physiology and behavior to the light-dark cycle, regulating sleep-wake timing, hormonal rhythms, metabolism and immunity. Among metabolic pathways tightly linked to circadian rhythm, tryptophan (Trp) metabolism occupies a central position because its catabolism through the kynurenine (Kyn) pathway, the serotonin (5-HT)-melatonin pathway and the microbiota-derived indole-AhR pathway, produce molecules endowed with significant neuro-modulatory and immunoregulatory activities and directly involved in circadian regulation. Emerging evidence supports a bidirectional relationship between the clock system and Trp metabolism. The molecular clock regulates expression and activity of key Trp enzymes, creating time-of-day variation in Trp flux, Kyn-Trp ratio, serotonin/melatonin synthesis and AhR ligands availability. Conversely, Trp-derived metabolites in turn modulate clock function and downstream physiology, such as diurnal variations in metabolism and immune response. Here we discuss recent studies highlighting how this interplay has important pathophysiological implications and disruption of Trp metabolism oscillatory pattern influences our susceptibility to developing diseases, such as infectious, metabolic and neuropsychiatric diseases. Moreover, we highlight the importance of considering daily fluctuation when using these molecules as biomarkers and interpreting them in a clinical setting. papers.title: Feedback Valence, Prediction Error, and the Limits of Computational Attribution in Symptom-Related EEG
papers.abstract: Feedback-locked electroencephalography (EEG) responses are often interpreted using model-derived prediction errors (PEs), although signed PE can be strongly coupled to feedback valence in binary-outcome tasks. We revisited a published anxiety-related EEG association using two open probabilistic-learning datasets to examine measurement reliability, predictor separability, and participant-level recovery. In the primary dataset, greater trait anxiety was associated with a larger negative-minus-positive FCz theta response among 46 participants with elevated depressive symptoms after adjustment for depression severity. The association also differed between the sampled depression-symptom groups. The feedback contrast showed useful within-session reliability, but matched delta and P3-minus-N2 analyses did not establish theta specificity. Within participants, feedback valence and signed PE were highly correlated (r = -0.964). Exact-design simulations showed that population-level model discrimination could succeed despite poor recovery of individual neural slopes. Participant-specific learning-model refits recovered overall signed PE more consistently than the within-valence variation needed to distinguish it from feedback valence. An independent dataset reproduced the FCz feedback contrast in untreated and placebo cohorts but lacked trait-anxiety scores. Adding signed PE to valence yielded a small held-out predictive improvement under one reinforcement-learning specification, with limited support across sessions and no comparable support under the dual-rate model or in placebo. Together, these findings support a symptom-related feedback EEG association while constraining its theta-specific and participant-level computational interpretation.

papers.title: Distinct Systemic Metabolic Remodeling and Neurobehavioral Deterioration in Chemotherapy-Treated Lung Cancer Models.
papers.abstract: Peripheral tumors and chemotherapy reshape host physiology, yet model selection for cancer-related neurobehavioral deterioration often remains empirical. In lung cancer, this deterioration often presents clinically as a somatic-psychological symptom cluster that includes fatigue, pain-related symptoms, sleep disturbance, and distress. We asked whether chemotherapy-treated subcutaneous and orthotopic Lewis lung carcinoma models reproduce a comparable symptom-related state or instead reflect distinct systemic and neurobehavioral contexts. Male C57BL/6J mice bearing subcutaneous tumors (STCG) or orthotopic tumors (OTCG), together with normal controls, were followed through chemotherapy using behavioral measures of fatigue-related performance, pain/discomfort responses, sleep-related responses, center-zone exploration and passive coping. These trajectories were interpreted alongside plasma metabolic profiles and targeted peripheral and brain pathological readouts. The two models diverged. STCG preserved survival and showed an active sickness-like pattern, including impaired rotarod performance, delayed sleep onset and a trend toward shortened thermal response latency. OTCG showed survival attrition, late-stage systemic deterioration, reduced thermal nociceptive responsiveness, prolonged pentobarbital-induced sleep duration and stronger behavioral suppression. Plasma metabolomics revealed broader remodeling in OTCG, involving ketone body, glutathione, one-carbon and redox-related pathways. Both tumor-bearing models showed peripheral oxidative stress and brain alterations involving Claudin-5, glial activation and synaptic markers. Exploratory within-model networks identified fatigue-related performance as a highly connected node, with differing behavioral and biological associations. These findings suggest that the two models capture complementary but non-interchangeable metabolic and neurobehavioral states under the tested chemotherapy conditions.

papers.title: A single day of natural daylight exposure and physical activity does not conclusively change circadian phase: A Bayesian crossover experiment
papers.abstract: Among the environmental signals that shape human physiology, the daily light-dark cycle is the primary zeitgeber of the human circadian system. Physical activity may provide an additional non-photic time cue and frequently co-occurs with daylight in everyday life. However, their independent and combined effects on circadian phase have rarely been disentangled under naturalistic daylight conditions. In a counterbalanced mixed-design experiment, 41 healthy adults (24 women; mean age = 23.7 years, SD = 4.3) participated in up to three 40-h visits on fixed individual sleep-wake schedules. Each visit comprised an 8-h exposure beginning 1.5 h after wake to natural daylight, daylight attenuated by amber-tinted glasses, or indoor electric light (within subjects; mean photopic illuminances: 1196, 460, and 75 lx), with otherwise dim-light conditions. Participants hiked for approximately 4 h or remained sedentary (between subjects; activity indexed by median heart rate reserve [HRR]; group means: 32.7% and 2.7%). Bayesian hierarchical models used individual photopic illuminance (ActTrust 2) and median HRR to predict change in dim-light melatonin onset (DLMO; primary outcome) and exploratory outcomes (daytime and evening sleepiness, mood, and wellbeing, daytime perceived exertion, and evening psychomotor vigilance). Per standard-deviation increase in log-transformed illuminance and median HRR, estimated DLMO changes were -4.22 min (95% HDI [-10.93, 2.22]; BF = 0.70) and -6.48 min (95% HDI [-13.79, 1.27], BF = 1.56), respectively. Evidence remained inconclusive for both predictors and their interaction. Exploratory findings were largely inconclusive, practically negligible, or favoured the absence of effects. The circadian effects of a single day of natural daylight exposure, with or without physical activity, therefore remain unclear. Resolving this question may require larger samples and brighter, repeated, or habitual exposure timed to phases of greater circadian light sensitivity.

papers.title: Multi-night evaluation of the Oura Ring in free-living older adults: App-reported sleep efficiency as an indicator of measurement stability.
papers.abstract: Consumer sleep trackers are increasingly used for long-term sleep monitoring, but evidence regarding their performance remains limited in older adults. Here, we evaluated agreement and night-to-night stability of sleep metrics derived from the Oura Ring against the Dreem 3 EEG headband in free-living older adults and examined whether Oura-determined sleep efficiency (SE) could indicate measurement stability. Forty-five older adults (mean age±SD: 74.4±2.4 years; 23 females) concurrently wore the Oura Ring Gen3 and Dreem 3 headband during habitual sleep at home, contributing 210 nights of paired recordings. Total sleep time (TST), SE, sleep onset latency (SOL), wake after sleep onset (WASO), and sleep stages were compared. Participants were stratified by average Oura-determined sleep efficiency across nights (≥85% versus <85%). Device agreement, epoch-by-epoch performance, and night-to-night variability in Oura-Dreem bias were assessed. Compared with Dreem 3, Oura underestimated TST (-14.6±35.7 min), SE (-2.9±6.7%), and REM sleep duration (-23.8±29.3 min), while overestimating SOL (11.4±16.8 min). Overall sleep/wake agreement was moderate (accuracy: 85.3±4.8%; sensitivity: 88.4±6.0%; kappa: 0.58±0.10). Critically, participants with lower average Oura-determined SE (<85%) demonstrated larger TST bias and lower sleep/wake agreement, accuracy, sensitivity, and kappa compared those with higher SE. Lower mean Oura-determined SE was also associated with greater night-to-night variability in Oura-Dreem bias, most notably for SOL (ρ=-0.30), with weaker associations for WASO (ρ=-0.19) and TST (ρ=-0.10). Oura-determined sleep efficiency may provide useful contextual information regarding measurement stability and help identify circumstances in which wearable-derived sleep metrics should be interpreted with greater caution.

papers.title: Cannabidiol and fronto-parietal EEG connectivity in autistic children.
papers.abstract: Autistic children often show altered brain network connectivity, including circuitry implicated in social cognition. Cannabidiol (CBD) has emerged as a potential therapy for autism, but its neural mechanisms remain under-researched. Here, we analyze resting-state data collected as part of a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial, to explore whether 12 weeks of oral CBD oil could modulate functional connectivity in autistic children. Twenty-nine autistic children (5 to 12 years) completed two 12-week intervention periods (CBD and placebo, randomized) separated by an 8-week washout. Before and after each period, 5 min of eyes-open resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) were obtained from a subset of 18 participants (8 female). Functional connectivity was calculated across 16 electrode-pairs in the delta, theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Beta-band connectivity between the right frontal and right inferior-parietal electrodes increased following CBD (P = 0.001, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected P [pFDR] = 0.022), and alpha connectivity showed an increase that did not remain following FDR correction (P = 0.036, pFDR = 0.428). No significant differences were observed following placebo for any frequency band (pFDR > 0.69). This study provides preliminary evidence that 12 weeks of cannabidiol is associated with an increase in right fronto-parietal (F4-P8) functional connectivity in autistic children, most pronounced in the beta-band. Replication in larger samples is needed to confirm generalizability and clinical relevance.

papers.title: Rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder as a model of early neurodegeneration: challenges for research and clinical diagnosis.
papers.abstract: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) has evolved from a descriptive parasomnia to a clinically informative model for studying early neurodegenerative processes, particularly within the spectrum of α-synucleinopathies. Defined by the loss of REM sleep atonia and the emergence of dream enactment behaviors, RBD reflects dysfunction of brainstem circuits that normally suppress motor output during dreaming. Longitudinal evidence indicates that many individuals with isolated RBD eventually develop neurodegenerative disease, most commonly Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, or, less frequently, multiple system atrophy, positioning RBD among the most specific clinical markers of prodromal synucleinopathy currently recognized. Mechanistic studies suggest that RBD arises from instability within distributed REM sleep regulatory networks involving dopaminergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic, and cholinergic systems. This network dysfunction may precede classic motor and cognitive symptoms and can be accompanied by early abnormalities in neurophysiology, imaging, cognition, olfaction, autonomic function, and molecular biomarkers. These findings support a model in which RBD may represent one of the earliest clinically accessible manifestations of a multisystem neurodegenerative process, although anatomical origin, propagation patterns, and phenoconversion trajectories vary across patients. Despite these advances, clinical management remains largely symptomatic, and key challenges persist in diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostic counselling, and therapeutic development. A broader clinical framework is therefore needed, in which RBD is not viewed solely as an isolated sleep disorder but also as a potential marker of early neurodegeneration in appropriately characterized patients. Integrating polysomnography with multimodal biomarkers and network-based models of disease may refine risk stratification and support the development of targeted interventions at earlier stages of neurodegenerative disease.

papers.title: Tick tock: how the body's circadian clock keeps cardiometabolic rhythm in check.
papers.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates the internal timing of numerous physiological processes through an approximately 24-h cycle. It comprises a hypothalamic central clock, which responds to light cues and entrains peripheral clocks within individual cells and organs that, depending on the tissue, regulate gene expression across diverse biological functions in a tissue-specific manner. Peripheral clocks are also entrained by feeding and exercise-related cues, enabling their synchronization with feeding rhythm and physiology. Together, these clocks maintain a complex molecular network essential for metabolic homeostasis. Disruption of circadian rhythms, driven by genetic, environmental, or behavioral factors, is increasingly recognized as a major contributor to cardiometabolic disorders. Modern lifestyles, including shift work, irregular sleep, prolonged exposure to artificial light at night, jet lag, and erratic eating schedules, misalign circadian clocks with environmental cues, contributing to disruption of circadian rhythms or chronodisruption. This misalignment alters hormonal regulation, promotes systemic inflammation, and impairs metabolic balance, thereby increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease, obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related complications. The present review examines the mechanistic roles of core circadian clock genes in cardiometabolic health, highlighting their regulation of physiological processes in peripheral organs such as the heart, liver, and adipose tissue. We further discuss how circadian clock disruption accelerates disease onset and progression and explore emerging therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological modulation of the molecular circadian clock components and personalized chronotherapy. These approaches offer promising avenues to restore circadian alignment and mitigate cardiometabolic risk.

papers.title: Information leakage and performance overestimation in EEG-based schizophrenia detection: evidence from literature and empirical analyses.
papers.abstract: Detecting schizophrenia (SZ) from electroencephalography (EEG) signals using machine- and deep learning models gained traction lately due to potential utility in early disease detection and differential diagnosis. Classification performance reports in the range of 95% accuracy and above are common; however, review of state-of-the-art literature indicates that ~65% of published works involve erroneous practices in the evaluation pipeline such as epoch- instead of subject-based data splitting or ranking and selecting features before data partitioning. The consequent information leakage can result in an overestimation of SZ detection performance. Here we explicitly test this on three open SZ-EEG datasets using gold standard classification approaches in leaky and leakage-free implementations. Results indicate that information leakage can inflate SZ classification accuracy by up to ~30%. Accordingly, best practices regarding EEG-based SZ detection must be established and promoted before this technology can be further developed into a clinical decision-making tool.

papers.title: Comparison between Three-Night and Single-Night Actigraphic Sleep Assessment During Early Hospitalization.
papers.abstract: To determine whether a single-night actigraphic sleep assessment during early hospitalization can approximate a 3-night average and characterize inpatient sleep- and rest-activity rhythm. Non-parametric circadian rhythm analysis (NPCRA) variables were reported descriptively. The 3-night mean sleep duration was 342 ± 83 minutes, with reduced sleep efficiency and increased fragmentation. No significant differences were observed between first-night values and 3-night averages for actual sleep time, mobile time, sleep efficiency, fragmentation index or average light exposure. Agreement was good for these parameters (ICC_single ≈ 0.71-0.75), whereas sleep latency showed lower reliability (ICC_single = 0.51). The Bland-Altman analysis demonstrated no systematic bias, with up to 6.3% of observations outside the 95% limits of agreement for most parameters and 9.4% for sleep latency. papers.title: Augmented cardiac growth hormone signaling in circadian-disrupted cardiomyopathy.
papers.abstract: Circadian disruption, including rotating shift work, social jet lag, and chronic sleep disturbance, is associated with increased cardiovascular risk and may promote cardiac remodeling. The molecular mechanisms connecting clock disruption to structural heart disease remain incompletely defined. This minireview advances the hypothesis that the growth hormone, GH, axis is an underrecognized endocrine mediator. GH secretion is time dependent, with most daily secretion occurring during early nocturnal sleep-in humans. Cardiomyocytes express GH receptors, and GH can activate Janus kinase 2, signal transducer and activator of transcription 5, phosphoinositide 3 kinase and Akt, and mitogen activated protein kinase and extracellular signal regulated kinase pathways that influence cardiac growth and metabolism. We propose that the cardiomyocyte molecular clock restricts GH responsiveness to circadian phases. REV ERBα is a plausible component of this restraint, but direct cardiomyocyte evidence is lacking. Circadian disruption may increase or mistime myocardial GH signaling, promoting hypertrophy, fibrosis, and metabolic inflexibility. The strongest support comes from cardiomyocyte specific Bmal1 deficient mice, which show increased GH induced cardiac STAT5 phosphorylation, increased cardiac Igf1 expression, and remodeling. Reduction of GH receptor gene dosage partially attenuates this phenotype, supporting a causal contribution of cardiac GH signaling. Nevertheless, genetic clock ablation is not equivalent to environmental circadian misalignment in shift work or chronic sleep disruption. We critically evaluate the components of this proposed clock-GH-heart axis, identify unresolved questions, and outline experiments and chronopharmacological strategies to test whether restoring temporal control of GH signaling can prevent pathological remodeling while preserving physiological GH action.

papers.title: Multiscale Neurodynamic Alterations in Major Depressive Disorder Revealed by Lempel-Ziv Complexity of Multi-Paradigm Resting-State EEG.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) abnormalities in major depressive disorder (MDD) have predominantly been examined through single-frequency band analyses or single-scale nonlinear measures, and largely within a single resting-state paradigm, which limits the characterization of regulatory interactions across temporal scales. In this study, we investigated dynamic transitions and integrative patterns of multiscale EEG activity in MDD across multiple resting-state paradigms, with a focus on characterizing alterations in multiscale neural dynamic organization. Based on multiscale Lempel-Ziv Complexity (LZC), we derived two classes of features quantifying the Scale-Dependent Variation Slope and the Cross-Scale Correlation Coefficient. Resting-state EEG from the MDD Patients and Healthy Controls EEG Data (MPHC) was analyzed under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions to compare multiscale regulatory dynamics between patients with MDD and healthy controls. Patients with MDD showed impaired complexity transitions from low to high frequencies and disrupted delta-centered cross-scale integration. Distinct coupling reconfiguration patterns emerged across resting states, indicating a systemic imbalance in multiscale integrative organization. Classification models built from statistically selected features performed consistently across Support Vector Machine, K-Nearest Neighbor, and Decision Tree algorithms, reaching a maximum accuracy of 85.71% with a balanced sensitivity-specificity profile. Convergent results across models further suggested the preliminary discriminative value of the proposed features within the present dataset. These findings provide a preliminary multiscale neurodynamic framework for EEG characterization in MDD and suggest that cross-scale integration differences may provide a quantitative basis for characterizing multiscale EEG dynamics in depression.

papers.title: Harnessing Neuroendocrine and Circadian Clocks in Beneficial Insects for Agricultural Chrono-Management.
papers.abstract: Pollinators and natural enemies provide essential agricultural ecosystem services that are regulated by circadian clocks, hormones, and biogenic amines. This review synthesizes research on the integration between neuroendocrine systems and circadian clocks across different taxa, identifying both conserved regulatory mechanisms and lineage-specific adaptive traits. These multilayered interactions coordinate insect behavior, life-history development, and the alignment of insect activities with available resources. We propose agricultural chrono-management, a framework to improve ecosystem services by using targeted environmental cues to align beneficial insect activity with farming schedules. However, most evidence so far comes from the laboratory and controlled studies, and field validation remains limited. We further evaluated the feasibility, ecological risks, and climate resilience of photoperiodic regulation, nutritional modulation, and synthetic ecological interventions. Key future research priorities include multiomics integration, large-scale field validation, and predictive modeling of ecosystem services. This synthesis links molecular-level regulatory mechanisms to ecological outcomes and establishes a foundational framework for climate-resilient management of beneficial insects.

papers.title: Resting-State EEG Graph Analysis Reveals Enhanced Alpha-Band Integration in High-IQ Individuals: The MENSA-Connect Project.
papers.abstract: To assess whether resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) connectivity differs between high-intelligence individuals (MENSA members) and controls using graph-theory metrics: clustering coefficient, characteristic path length, and small-worldness. Resting-state 64-channel EEG data were recorded in 29 MENSA participants and 20 controls. Functional connectivity was estimated using Lagged Linear Coherence across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Graph-theory measures were computed using sLORETA and the Brain Connectivity Toolbox. Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann-Whitney U test; p-values were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) procedure, and effect sizes with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Compared with controls, MENSA participants showed significantly lower characteristic path length in the alpha band (Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) critical value = 0.004), indicating greater global network integration. In the beta band, they showed a higher clustering coefficient (BH critical value = 0.008), reflecting greater local specialization; together with a higher characteristic path length (BH critical value = 0.013), suggesting reduced global communication. No significant group differences were observed in small-worldness across frequency bands. High-Intelligence Quotient (IQ) individuals show a frequency-dependent resting-state cortical organization, characterized by enhanced alpha-band integration and increased beta-band local specialization. These findings support a nuanced neural-efficiency model of intelligence without changes in small-world architecture. Given the cross-sectional and observational design, these findings should be regarded as associative rather than causal and require replication in larger, independent samples. These findings indicate frequency-specific differences in functional network organization, although their cognitive implications remain to be established.

papers.title: Personalized Postoperative Pain Management and Therapies Based on Pharmacogenomics.
papers.abstract: Postoperative pain management must account for differences in drug metabolism, pain phenotype, prior opioid exposure, psychosocial vulnerability, and cognitive function. This narrative review proposes a staged precision-medicine framework separating clinically actionable pharmacogenomics from heterogeneous risk modifiers and investigational adjuncts. The strongest actionable guidance concerns CYP2D6-guided codeine and tramadol prescribing. Other genetic markers require interpretation alongside procedure-specific pain, comorbidities, medication exposure, and patient preferences rather than use as deterministic prescribing rules. Dopamine-related pathways provide a mechanistic link between pain, reward, motivation, and attention. Parkinson disease illustrates dopamine-pain interactions but is not a direct model of postoperative pain. Reward Deficiency Syndrome, the Genetic Addiction Risk Severity/Score, and the Reward Deficiency Syndrome Questionnaire-29 are considered exploratory constructs rather than validated tools for postoperative prescribing. The Continuous Visual Attention Test may offer objective neurocognitive monitoring through reaction time, response variability, and error measures. These measures are not pain-specific and require interpretation in the context of anesthesia, opioids, sedatives, sleep disruption, mood, delirium, baseline cognition, and pain intensity. Prospective studies should determine whether integrating clinical assessment, established pharmacogenomic guidance, and investigational behavioral and neurocognitive measures improves pain outcomes, opioid requirements, adherence, functional recovery, and safety. The framework defines research priorities and implementation endpoints while preserving multimodal analgesia, opioid stewardship, and clinical judgment as the foundation of care.

papers.title: Physiological insights and clinical evidence of high flow nasal cannula as first-line therapy for acute hypercapnic exacerbation of COPD: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a common lung disease. Acute exacerbations (AECOPD) are associated with increased hospitalisations and mortality. Current guidelines provide only conditional recommendation for the use of High Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) supported by low-certainty evidence in hypercapnic respiratory failure. Since then, additional studies have been published, and we aimed to review the available literature on HFNC as a first-line therapy in hypercapnic AECOPD. Structured literature research was performed in PubMed and Embase to include studies assessing HFNC as a first-line therapy in hypercapnic AECOPD and focusing on clinical outcomes (dyspnoea, blood gas, treatment failure, mortality). Studies were categorized as single-arm studies, comparisons with conventional oxygen therapy (COT), or comparisons with non-invasive ventilation (NIV). Among 17 articles included, 2 were uncontrolled, 3 articles compared HFNC to COT and 12 compared HFNC to NIV. HFNC was often associated with better comfort and tolerance. Compared to COT, HFNC might reduce treatment failure, but evidence is still scarce. Compared to NIV, HFNC had similar effects on dyspnoea and blood gas analysis in most studies, but it remains uncertain considering treatment failure. In hypercapnic AECOPD, HFNC remains an alternative therapeutic option as compared to COT but also to NIV when the latter is contraindicated, not tolerated or during breaks from NIV. Further research is warranted with well-designed RCT focusing on treatment failure and mortality. In the future, patients might be selected considering some endotypes of AECOPD such as bronchorrhea, sleep apnea overlap or disproportionate dyspnoea which could benefit differently from HFNC.

papers.title: Time use diaries as a tool for measuring sleep among individuals incarcerated.
papers.abstract: To evaluate the feasibility of using time use diaries to measure sleep and characterize sleep duration and sleep-wake patterns among individuals incarcerated in jail. Adults housed in 2 general‑population units of a Southwestern US jail completed a 4‑day, paper‑and‑pencil time use diary documenting 10-minute activity intervals. Sleep was identified using participant‑reported activities coded with the Compendium of Physical Activities. Sleep was categorized as day- or night-time based on facility schedules. Sleep pattern indicators, including wake‑time, return‑to‑sleep behavior, napping, and bedtime, were classified across valid diary days. Descriptive statistics summarized sleep duration and patterns overall and by sex assigned at jail intake. Of 64 participants, 62 (96.9%) completed at least one valid diary day; most completed all days, yielding 238 diary days (93.0% completion). Participants averaged 630.8 minutes (10.5 hours) of total daily sleep, with 256.7 minutes (4.3 hours) of daytime sleep and 374.1 minutes (6.2 hours) of nighttime sleep. Females and males had similar total sleep duration. Over half (56.5%) of participants' sleep patterns were not aligned with institutional schedules for programming, meals, and lights out; 83.9% returned to sleep after breakfast (4:30 AM); and 53.2% napped during the day. Half of participants went to bed at lockdown (9:00 PM), while 27.4% went to bed after lockdown. Females with job assignments slept substantially less overall than females without. Time use diaries are feasible and informative for measuring sleep among individuals incarcerated in jail. Sleep was fragmented and disproportionately accumulated during the day, reflecting structural constraints of the carceral environment. Findings underscore the need for sleep‑measurement tools tailored to carceral settings.

papers.title: Tetramelic Monodactyly With Neonatal Encephalopathy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Congenital limb defects are etiologically heterogeneous congenital malformations, with genetic causes being one of the major contributors. We report a neonate with limb anomalies and severe encephalopathy in whom rapid trio whole-genome sequencing identified a pathogenic duplication at 10q24.31q24.32. A near-term male neonate presented with bilateral radial and tibial ray aplasia, with preserved ulnar and fibular elements, resulting in tetramelic monodactyly of the fifth digits. Family history revealed an apparent autosomal dominant pattern, with the patient's father and older sister similarly affected. In the first days of life, the patient developed unexplained apnea, respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, and severe diffuse encephalopathy on continuous EEG monitoring. Brain MRI, head ultrasound, and metabolic workup were unremarkable. Echocardiography showed normal cardiac anatomy. Trio rapid whole-genome sequencing demonstrated a 10q24 duplication, a locus previously associated with split-hand/foot malformation. This genetic variant in this family leads to tetramelic monodactyly of the fifth digits across at least two generations.

papers.title: Tirzepatide for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea: from apnea-hypopnea index reduction to cardiometabolic risk mitigation-a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a chronic respiratory disorder with nocturnal oxygen desaturation that is often associated with multisystemic sequelae such as hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, and increased morbidity and mortality. Obesity has been proposed as a modifiable risk factor; hence, the recent shift in focus to investigating anti-obesity medications for the management of OSA. Tirzepatide is the first U.S. FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for the treatment of moderate-to-severe OSA in adults with obesity to be utilized in combination with low caloric intake and physical activity, given its prior success in managing type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity. This narrative review evaluates tirzepatide and the SURMOUNT-OSA trial program as the key contemporary anchors for the pharmacological treatment of OSA in adults with concurrent obesity. Because the randomized evidence base currently comprises a single pivotal trial program, the review centers on SURMOUNT-OSA and its prespecified endpoints along with post hoc analyses, supplemented by observational, modeling, and mechanistic studies. In the SURMOUNT-OSA program, tirzepatide produced randomized, placebo-controlled reductions in the apnea-hypopnea index, sleep apnea-specific hypoxic burden, body weight, and systemic inflammation. The program was designed around respiratory and metabolic endpoints rather than clinical events, so it cannot support conclusions about mortality, cardiovascular, or renal outcomes. Favorable signals for those events, including all-cause mortality, major adverse kidney events, and major adverse cardiovascular events, come only from nonrandomized observational cohorts and are best regarded as directional and exploratory rather than definitive. Tirzepatide may help frame OSA as a multifactorial and partially metabolically treatable disease and may represent a clinically meaningful expansion of treatment options alongside, rather than as a replacement for, established mechanical and procedural therapies. The available evidence is anchored in a single phase 3 trial program and limited by short follow-up and the absence of definitive comparative and long-term outcome data. Long-term durability of effect after discontinuation, generalizability beyond the SURMOUNT-OSA-eligible population, OSA-specific economic analysis, and head-to-head comparisons against CPAP remain the principal unsettled questions requiring dedicated long-term studies before firm clinical recommendations can be made.

papers.title: The Applied Sport Science of Professional Male Basketball: A Narrative Review of Current and Emerging Practices.
papers.abstract: Basketball is a physically demanding intermittent team sport which requires a multifaceted approach to optimise player preparation, performance, health, and recovery. Quantifying the training and match demands of professional basketball players can help practitioners develop effective strategies for managing fatigue, monitoring training loads, and guiding physical preparation. Sleep and travel disruptions present additional challenges to practitioners and can have deleterious effects on recovery and readiness to compete. Nutrition is also an essential component supporting performance and recovery and should be individualised to the needs of each player. The inherent complexity of basketball requires practitioners to develop a holistic view that considers the interaction between tactical, technical, psychological, and physical basketball-related factors along with external factors from the greater basketball system (e.g., players, coaches, support staff, organisations, schedules, referees, and governing bodies) that can influence performance. Advances in technology continue to shape performance monitoring, injury-risk forecasting, and training methodologies, yet practitioners must be aware of potential risks such as player privacy concerns and the misuse of data. A comprehensive understanding of these factors provides valuable insights for practitioners to develop effective evidence-based strategies and frameworks for working with professional male basketball players.
